prompt: A stateless branch router lets replies from web servers into the LAN with tcp sport 443 accept. An auditor tests it from outside with a connection from source port 443 to port 3389 on a LAN machine. What does the router do?

choices.text: Drops it, since no LAN machine asked for that connection first
choices.why: A stateless filter keeps no record of who asked.

choices.text: Drops it, since 3389 is not a port the rule names
choices.why: The rule names no destination port at all.

choices.text: Lets it through: the rule tests a number the sender chose
choices.why: Right. The source port is written by the sender, and the rule cannot tell a reply from anything else carrying it.

choices.text: Lets the first packet through, then drops the rest of it
choices.why: It learns nothing; each packet is judged alone, and each carries source port 443.

prompt: fw is replaced by a stricter firewall that marks a packet met in mid-stream as invalid. It restarts while laptop has a connection open to app on 8080. What happens to that connection?

choices.text: It continues, because a rule would have let it start
choices.why: That is Linux's default, the 1 in nf_conntrack_tcp_loose; this firewall is the stricter kind.

choices.text: It continues, because an established entry is kept for five days
choices.why: The five days are in memory, and a restart forgets everything in it.

choices.text: It breaks: its next packet matches no entry
choices.why: Right. The table was lost in the restart, so the packet is invalid and dropped.

choices.text: It continues once app resends its last reply, which recreates the entry
choices.why: An entry is created when a rule accepts a new packet, and replies from the servers start nothing.

prompt: Under the lesson's counted stateful rule set, laptop fetches app's health page five times, each over a new TCP connection. How many packets does the ct state new rule count?
A provider's border router carries millions of flows in front of a company's stateful firewall. Which rule belongs on the router?

choices.text: Drop internet packets with a private source
choices.why: Right. That can never be legitimate and needs no memory to decide.

choices.text: Accept packets that belong to connections the staff opened
choices.why: That needs a table of connections, which a stateless router does not keep.

choices.text: Drop SSH travelling on port 443
choices.why: Telling SSH from TLS means reading the payload, which is lesson 2's layer.

choices.text: Accept replies by matching their source port
choices.why: That is the return-rule hole this lesson walked through.

prompt: A stateful rule set lets the LAN ask dns on UDP 53, with established,related accepted first. laptop asks one question, and the answer arrives 45 seconds later. What happens to the answer?

choices.text: It passes as established, since the entry lasts five days
choices.why: Five days is an established TCP connection; a single UDP exchange is forgotten after 30 seconds.

choices.text: It passes as related, being an answer to a known question
choices.why: related is a new flow tied to an entry that exists, such as an ICMP error; this entry is gone.

choices.text: It passes, since a UDP flow is kept for 120 seconds
choices.why: 120 applies once the flow has become a stream, with packets going back and forth more than once.

choices.text: Dropped: after 30 quiet seconds the flow is forgotten
choices.why: Right. The answer then starts a new conversation from the DMZ, and no rule lets one start there.

prompt: Suricata's flow record for a connection from desk to 203.0.113.77 shows dest_port 443 and app_proto ssh. What does that record establish?

choices.text: The TLS handshake failed, so Suricata fell back to guessing
choices.why: It named the protocol from the SSH greeting it read, not from a guess.

choices.text: The port rule refused the connection
choices.why: A flow with an application named means the conversation took place.

choices.text: An SSH conversation used the port kept open for HTTPS
choices.why: Right. Suricata recognised SSH by its first bytes, whatever the port.

choices.text: What desk typed after logging in, read from the session
choices.why: After the key exchange SSH is encrypted; the greeting lines are what is readable.

prompt: The rule alert tls $HOME_NET any -> any !443 (msg:"TLS on a port other than 443"; flow:to_server,established; tls.sni; content:"."; sid:1000002; rev:1;) is loaded. Which of these connections from laptop raise an alert? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: TLS to a server on port 8443, naming shop.example.net
choices.why: Right. TLS, a port other than 443, and a name with a dot.

choices.text: TLS to www on port 443, naming www.example.com
choices.why: !443 excludes exactly this one.

choices.text: SSH to remote on port 443
choices.why: It is SSH, not TLS, and it goes to 443; lesson 2's other rule is the one that fires.

choices.text: TLS to a mail server on port 993, naming mail.example.com
choices.why: Right. Any TLS off 443 with a server name matches.

choices.text: Plain HTTP to app on port 8080
choices.why: HTTP is not TLS, so there is no SNI to match.

prompt: A company turns on TLS inspection, and its firewall accepts server certificates a browser would reject. What changes for a member of staff visiting a site with a bad certificate?

choices.text: The browser warns as before, since it checks the real certificate
choices.why: The browser sees the certificate the firewall made, not the real one.

choices.text: No warning: the firewall re-signs the site
choices.why: Right. The firewall now decides validity, and the company's authority vouches for whatever it accepted.

choices.text: The site fails to load, because the firewall lacks the server's private key
choices.why: The firewall makes its own certificate for the name and needs no server key; the key problem is the client certificate's.

choices.text: The certificate crosses in clear, and the firewall logs a warning
choices.why: In TLS 1.3 the certificate is encrypted, and a log line warns nobody at the keyboard.

prompt: Against TLS 1.3 an inspector still reads the name the client puts in its first message, the field abbreviated ___.
A team switches a new WAF straight to blocking on a Monday. By noon the support form and the checkout return 403 to ordinary customers. What did the lesson's rollout do that this skipped?

choices.text: Raised the paranoia level so more is caught before blocking
choices.why: Higher levels block more legitimate traffic, not less.

choices.text: Ran it detection-only first, reading what it would block
choices.why: Right. Seeing its verdicts on real traffic comes before letting it refuse anything.

choices.text: Removed the rules that matched those two forms across the site
choices.why: That turns protection off everywhere; the lesson's fix was one rule, one field, one location.

choices.text: Put the WAF behind the application
choices.why: It sits on the proxy, where TLS ends and before the application.

prompt: Match each response to the support-form false positive with what it switches off.

pairs.right: blocking by every rule, on the whole site
SQL detection in every field of every page
one rule, for one field, at one location

right_distractors: the XSS rules for the comment field

prompt: A WAF appliance is placed in front of www and passes the encrypted connections through untouched, so TLS still ends on www. What can its rules inspect in the requests?

choices.text: The paths but not the bodies, since headers travel in clear
choices.why: In HTTPS the path and the headers are encrypted as well.

choices.text: The whole request, since it sits in front of the proxy
choices.why: Being in front is not enough; a WAF has to be where TLS ends.

choices.text: The whole request, once it has read www's certificate
choices.why: A certificate is public; reading it decrypts nothing.

choices.text: Nothing of them: they are still encrypted as they cross it
choices.why: Right. That is why the lesson's WAF runs on the proxy that terminates TLS.

prompt: The shop's proxy has client_max_body_size 16k, which the lesson reads as 16 KiB. What is the largest request body it accepts, in bytes?
The application on app has to call a payment provider at 198.51.100.7 on port 443, and the servers row of the matrix is empty. Which change keeps the matrix's discipline?

choices.text: Let the servers segment reach the internet on 443
choices.why: That lets every server reach every site; a server that calls out gets one destination.

choices.text: Move app into the DMZ, which faces the internet
choices.why: The DMZ has no row towards the internet either, and app would lose the zone that protects it.

choices.text: A new cell: app to 198.51.100.7 on 443, with a comment
choices.why: Right. One source, one destination, one port, and a comment naming the decision.

choices.text: Route the calls through www, which already reaches app
choices.why: That rule lets www start conversations with app, not the other way round.

prompt: Match each network design to what it means for segmentation.

pairs.right: a wrong rule can open every zone at once
a flaw opens one layer and the other still stands

pairs.left: VLANs routed by the core switch
pairs.right: traffic between zones meets no rule
each conversation between zones needs a rule

right_distractors: machines inside one VLAN are filtered from each other

prompt: Which of these additions to fw's rules make the blast radius of a compromised www larger? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: www to the internet on 443, so it can fetch updates
choices.why: Right. A new rule starting in the DMZ, and the one a callback needs.

choices.text: admin to www on SSH
choices.why: It starts in the management zone, not in the DMZ.

choices.text: www to db on 5432, for a cache of prices
choices.why: Right. A second door from the DMZ, straight to the database.

choices.text: the internet to www on port 8443
choices.why: It starts on the internet; it changes what reaches www, not what www reaches.

prompt: A mail relay, mail, is added to the DMZ and runs an SSH server. No rule is changed. From admin, what does probe mail:22 print?

choices.text: blocked, because each rule names its destination address
choices.why: The administration rule names oifname { "eth1", "eth3" } and no address.

choices.text: refused, because no rule mentions mail yet
choices.why: refused means nothing listens; mail runs SSH and the rule lets the packet through.

choices.text: blocked until the zone matrix gets an entry for mail
choices.why: The matrix is the document; the rule loaded on fw is what decides.

choices.text: open: the rule names the DMZ's interface
choices.why: Right. Any machine that joins the DMZ inherits the management cell's SSH.

prompt: A resolver on the internet asks dns about www.example.com, gets an answer too large for UDP, and retries over TCP. Under baseline.nft, what happens to the retry?

choices.text: Blocked: the internet's DNS cell allows UDP
choices.why: Right. The staff's cell names both transports; the internet's names UDP alone.

choices.text: Answered, since DNS falls back to TCP for large answers
choices.why: DNS does, but the firewall decides by the cell, and this cell is UDP.

choices.text: Answered, since the UDP question left a conntrack entry behind
choices.why: The TCP connection is a new conversation with an entry of its own.

choices.text: Refused by dns itself
choices.why: The packet does not reach dns; fw drops it, which probe reports as blocked.

prompt: A company replaces its blocklist with a deny-by-default rule set built from its zone matrix. What should it expect in the first week?

choices.text: A quiet week, as whatever worked before still works
choices.why: Deny by default refuses what is not named, and some legitimate traffic was forgotten.

choices.text: New services exposed until somebody lists them
choices.why: That was the blocklist's failure; now an unlisted service is blocked.

choices.text: Complaints about legitimate traffic that nobody listed
choices.why: Right. The allowlist's failure is loud and fixed within the day.

choices.text: Drop logs of attacks it used to miss, and no complaints
choices.why: The loud failure is the legitimate traffic refused, and people say so.

prompt: Monitoring on admin, 192.168.99.10, has to read metrics that fw itself serves on TCP port 9100. Where does the rule go?

choices.text: forward: from eth4 to fw's address, tcp dport 9100, accept
choices.why: forward sees traffic crossing fw; traffic addressed to fw meets input.

choices.text: input: iifname eth4, ip saddr 192.168.99.10, tcp dport 9100, new, accept
choices.why: Right. The management interface and the one source, like the SSH rule beside it.

choices.text: input: tcp dport 9100 accept, with no interface or source
choices.why: That lets every zone read fw's metrics.

choices.text: output: fw sends the metrics, so its own chain allows them
choices.why: admin starts the conversation; fw's replies pass as established.

prompt: Order the rules of a deny-by-default forward chain from top to bottom, as this lesson arranges them.
items: ct state established,related accept
ct state invalid drop
the commented accept rules for new conversations
the rate-limited log rule
trap: A log rule anywhere but last records traffic that later rules would have accepted.

A flood of 3,000 unfinished handshakes a second crosses fw, and each entry has seen the SYN-ACK. With nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_syn_recv set to 20 as in the lesson, how many such entries does the table hold once it is steady?
With tcp_syncookies = 1 and the queue of half-open connections full, order what happens when a real client connects to www.
items: the client's SYN arrives
www encodes what it would remember into its SYN-ACK's sequence number
www forgets the connection
the client's ACK brings the number back and www checks it
www builds the connection
trap: The server keeps nothing between its SYN-ACK and the ACK; the number carries it.

prompt: The shop slows down. The link is at 30%, conntrack -C is far below the maximum, and the proxy logs thousands of well-formed searches a second, each source asking a few times. Where is this absorbed?

choices.text: Upstream, at the provider or a scrubbing service
choices.why: The link is not full, so this is not volumetric.

choices.text: The firewall's per-source connection limit
choices.why: Each source asks a few times, which a per-source limit sees as normal.

choices.text: The proxy, the application and a cache
choices.why: Right. It is exhausting the application's work, which is the application kind.

choices.text: SYN cookies on www, with shorter timeouts on fw
choices.why: The handshakes complete, and neither the queue nor the table is filling.

prompt: A shop's link carries 1 Gbit/s, and attacks of 40 Gbit/s have hit others in its sector. Which measure answers that kind of attack?

choices.text: A firewall with a 40 Gbit/s interface in the building
choices.why: The flood is lost on the provider's side of the 1 Gbit/s link before it reaches the building.

choices.text: Shorter syn_recv timeouts and SYN cookies
choices.why: Those protect tables; a full link drops packets before they reach one.

choices.text: A per-source limit of four connections
choices.why: Each of thousands of sources stays under it, and the link fills anyway.

choices.text: A scrubbing service or a CDN, contracted before any attack
choices.why: Right. Capacity somebody else has, arranged in a meeting rather than during the incident.

prompt: Dynamic ARP inspection is on in every access switch. The gateway, 192.168.10.1, has its address set by hand rather than by DHCP. What else does the switch need, so that a machine on another port claiming the gateway's address is dropped?

choices.text: Port security limiting that port to one MAC address
choices.why: Port security counts MAC addresses; a machine lying in ARP presents one, its own.

choices.text: A static binding of the gateway's address
choices.why: Right. The snooping table learns from DHCP, and the gateway never asked DHCP for anything.

choices.text: The gateway's MAC learnt in the forwarding table, which the inspection reads
choices.why: The inspection checks answers against the DHCP snooping table, not the table of which MAC sits behind which port.

choices.text: arpwatch on the segment, reporting the pairing
choices.why: arpwatch reports a change after it happened; it drops no packet.

prompt: A compromised laptop poisons ARP on the staff LAN and relays its colleagues' traffic on to the gateway. They use the shop over HTTPS, and their browsers check the certificate. What does the laptop obtain from that traffic?

choices.text: Their session cookies, which pass through its interface
choices.why: They pass through encrypted: the HTTPS capture held no Cookie line at all.

choices.text: The paths of the pages requested, since TLS hides the body and not the request line
choices.why: The request line is inside TLS too: the sensor counted zero GET lines.

choices.text: Names, timing and sizes
choices.why: Right. Metadata survives; what was said does not.

choices.text: The passwords typed at sign-in, before TLS starts
choices.why: TLS is set up before any request is sent, the sign-in included.

prompt: Customers sign in to the shop from cafés and hotels. Which measures still protect their session cookie on those networks? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The Secure attribute, with the whole site on HTTPS and HSTS
choices.why: Right. The cookie never travels in clear, whatever the network.

choices.text: Dynamic ARP inspection on the company's office switches
choices.why: It protects the office's segments; a café's Wi-Fi is not one of them.

choices.text: A short lifetime, with a new value issued at sign-in
choices.why: Right. A copied cookie stops working soon.

choices.text: An arpwatch sensor on the staff LAN
choices.why: It watches the company's segment, not the customer's.

choices.text: Invalidating the session on the server at sign-out
choices.why: Right. The value dies with the session.

prompt: A machine on a switched network hears traffic addressed to others. Match each finding to the cause the lesson gives.

pairs.left: the administrators set up a SPAN port for the IDS sensor
pairs.right: a mirror port, arranged on purpose

pairs.left: the desk port has presented hundreds of MAC addresses
pairs.right: an overflowed address table, flooding like a hub

pairs.left: colleagues' neighbour tables list the gateway at that machine's MAC
pairs.right: ARP spoofing by that machine

right_distractors: a resolver answering for names it does not serve

prompt: With the fib rule loaded on fw, its counter starts climbing every night. A capture on the LAN shows the dropped packets all come from one workstation's MAC, each carrying a different source address from outside the company. What does this point to?

choices.text: The filter is dropping honest traffic and is better loosened to rp_filter 2
choices.why: Honest LAN traffic carries a LAN source, and fw has a route back to it through that interface.

choices.text: Somebody on the internet is forging the company's addresses
choices.why: These packets arrive on the LAN interface, on their way out.

choices.text: The workstation's own NAT is rewriting its source
choices.why: NAT is done at fw, and it writes one public address, not a different one each time.

choices.text: That workstation has been taken over and is joining somebody's flood with forged sources
choices.why: Right. Random forged sources are how a flood hides, and the egress filter made it visible.

prompt: The shop's zone is signed and the company's resolver validates. Somebody on the path between the resolver and the zone's name server replaces the address in an answer with their own. What does a client of the resolver receive?

choices.text: The forged address, handed over without the ad flag
choices.why: A validating resolver hands over nothing when the signature fails; that output is what +cd shows.

choices.text: The real address, rebuilt from the RRSIG
choices.why: A signature proves an answer; it does not carry the address to restore.

choices.text: SERVFAIL, and no address handed to the client
choices.why: Right. The signature does not match, so the resolver refuses.

choices.text: The forged address, because on the path the attacker's answer arrives first
choices.why: Winning the race is exactly what DNSSEC makes useless.

prompt: A resolver draws a random 16-bit transaction ID for each question and a random source port out of 1,000. By the lesson's arithmetic, one forged answer has one chance in how many of matching both?
On fw each network lives behind exactly one interface, so the kernel's reverse path check fits it as net.ipv4.conf.eth0.rp_filter = ___ .
desk is quarantined at fw with the inserted rule, yet shares on a workstation beside it, on the same staff LAN, keep being encrypted from desk. Why, and what closes that path?

choices.text: The rule missed desk's open connections; flushing conntrack at fw
choices.why: The rule matches on the source address in any state, and fw sees none of this traffic anyway.

choices.text: fw never sees it; host firewalls, or shutting desk's switch port
choices.why: Right. Two machines on one segment talk past the firewall.

choices.text: It sits in the wrong chain; moving it to input
choices.why: input is for traffic to fw itself; neither chain sees this traffic.

choices.text: desk took a new address; quarantining that one too
choices.why: Whatever the address, a rule at fw does not see traffic inside the segment.

prompt: Each night the file server copies its data into a shared folder on the backup server, with an account allowed to write there. Ransomware takes over the file server. What happens to the backups, and which design would have prevented it?

choices.text: Safe: the backup server runs another operating system
choices.why: The software writes through the share; the system on the other side does not matter.

choices.text: Safe for as long as the scheduled restore tests keep passing
choices.why: A restore test says the backup worked last time; it does not stop tonight's encryption.

choices.text: Overwritten too; copies pulled by another machine, with no write access from the source
choices.why: Right. Whatever a client can write, the software on it can overwrite.

choices.text: Overwritten too; a longer retention in the same shared folder
choices.why: Older copies in a folder the client can write are within its reach as well.

prompt: A host firewall is being written for every staff workstation, on the lesson's reasoning. Which rules belong in it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An input policy of drop
choices.why: Right. Allow what is used, drop the rest.

choices.text: File sharing on 445 accepted from the staff LAN, for colleagues' folders
choices.why: A workstation should not serve files; files live on servers.

choices.text: Accept for connections in state established or related
choices.why: Right. That is how the workstation's own connections come back.

choices.text: Remote desktop on 3389 accepted from the staff LAN, for support calls
choices.why: Support works from the management segment, and the staff LAN is where spreading happens.

choices.text: Remote desktop accepted from the management segment
choices.why: Right. That is where support works.

prompt: Order these controls by the stage of the attack where each one stands in the way, from earliest to latest.
items: the mail gateway's verdict on the message
protective DNS refusing the phishing page's name

prompt: Two sites agree a key with X25519, exchanging their public keys by e-mail, and nobody compares them through any other channel. What does the resulting encryption protect against?

choices.text: Both, since the private keys stayed at home
choices.why: A swapped public key makes you share a secret with the swapper, perfectly encrypted.

choices.text: Neither, because the public keys crossed the network in clear
choices.why: Public keys are meant to be seen; seeing them does not give the secret.

choices.text: A recorder of the traffic, but not somebody who swapped a key on the way
choices.why: Right. Key agreement proves nothing about whose key you hold.

choices.text: A swapper, since the two derived secrets would differ and the link would fail
choices.why: Each side shares a matching secret with the swapper, and nothing fails.

prompt: A web server's processor saturates when thousands of new visitors arrive at once, but not while a few clients download large files. By the lesson's measurements, which operation is the first suspect?

choices.text: AES-256-GCM encrypting the pages sent
choices.why: It ran at about 12.5 GB a second on one core, and large downloads would load it first.

choices.text: The RSA-2048 signature in each new handshake
choices.why: Right. 3,313 a second, once per connection: many new connections feel it first.

choices.text: RSA verification, which the server runs for each visitor
choices.why: Verification is the cheap side, 57,718 a second, and it is the client that verifies the server.

choices.text: 600,000 PBKDF2 rounds for each connection's key
choices.why: Those rounds were openssl enc turning a key file into a key, not part of TLS.

prompt: In the lesson's openssl enc command the key file holds 32 random bytes. A colleague proposes raising -iter from 600,000 to 6,000,000 to make the file safer. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: It makes the file ten times harder to open for whoever steals the key file
choices.why: With the key file in hand, decryption costs a little more time and then works.

choices.text: It gives CBC the tamper detection it lacks
choices.why: Key derivation says nothing about a changed ciphertext; an AEAD tag does.

choices.text: Rounds slow the guessing of a typed password; 32 random bytes are not guessed
choices.why: Right. The lesson says the rounds cost nothing here, and they buy nothing either.

choices.text: It raises the key to 2,560 bits
choices.why: Rounds change the cost of deriving the key, not its length.

pairs.right: the handshake's opening message
the handshake's reply
an empty keepalive
the branch's request and its answer, under ChaCha20-Poly1305

prompt: A vendor publishes MD5 digests of its firmware on a separate page that nobody else can edit. By the lesson, what do those digests still protect against?

choices.text: Accidental corruption
choices.why: Right. Collisions have been shown for MD5, so it no longer holds where somebody tries to fool the check.

choices.text: Tampering by anybody, because the page is separate from the file
choices.why: The separate page settles where the digest comes from; MD5 itself has demonstrated collisions.

choices.text: Little, since an MD5 digest can be reversed back into the firmware
choices.why: Collisions were shown, not reversal; and it still catches corruption.

choices.text: Tampering, because MD5 uses a key the vendor holds
choices.why: A hash has no key; anybody can compute one.

prompt: Staff laptops got release.pub from the internal wiki when the agent was installed. Months later the download server is taken over, and agent-2.4.2.tar.gz and its .sig are replaced with a file and a signature made with the attacker's own key. What do the laptops see when they verify?

choices.text: Signature Verified Successfully, since the signature matches the file it came with
choices.why: It matches the attacker's key, not the one on the laptops.

choices.text: Success, unless SHA256SUMS was changed too
choices.why: The signature check does not read the digest list.

choices.text: A question asking whether to trust the new key, as SSH asks
choices.why: openssl pkeyutl checks against the key it is given and asks nothing.

choices.text: Signature Verification Failure
choices.why: Right. The key on the laptops never left admin's control.

prompt: A developer stores each password as SHA-256 over a random per-user salt followed by the password, with the salt kept beside the value. What does the lesson say is still wrong?

choices.text: The salt should be one value shared by the users, so logins can be checked
choices.why: A shared salt lets one computation be compared against every account at once.

choices.text: SHA-256 is fast, so each guess at a stolen value is cheap
choices.why: Right. It needs a slow function: Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with many rounds.

choices.text: With the salt known, SHA-256 reverses
choices.why: Preimage resistance holds; the attack is guessing, fast.

choices.text: A salt stored beside the value reveals the password to a thief
choices.why: The salt is not secret; its job is to make each account its own computation.

prompt: When a third party has to check who produced a message, an HMAC falls short, because both sides hold the key; what fits is a digital ___.

items: make the Ed25519 key pair, once, on admin
publish release.pub somewhere users already trust
sign each release with the private key
on laptop, verify the download against the key obtained earlier

prompt: The certificate for app.corp.example.com runs from 28 September to 28 December 2026, both at midnight. How many days is it valid for?
A company CA with no name constraints is installed on every staff laptop, and its issuing CA's key is stolen. What can the thief do against those laptops?

choices.text: Impersonate the company's internal names, such as app.corp.example.com
choices.why: Without name constraints the key vouches for any name, public ones included.

choices.text: Present a trusted certificate for any name, public sites included
choices.why: Right. That is the risk a name constraint removes.

choices.text: Decrypt recordings of past sessions to company servers
choices.why: A CA's key signs certificates; it holds no session keys.

choices.text: Revoke the root, taking the laptops' trust away
choices.why: The issuing CA cannot revoke its parent, and the root's key is offline.

prompt: An internal client checks the issuing CA's CRL. Its cached copy passed its Next Update yesterday, and the CA's server cannot be reached. What does the lesson say a company should make that client do?

choices.text: Refuse the connection until a fresh list is fetched
choices.why: Right. Inside the company the CA controls both ends, so clients can check and refuse when they cannot.

choices.text: Carry on with the cached list, since the CA signed it

choices.text: ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384

prompt: A user on hostile café Wi-Fi returns to four sites visited last week. Which site leaves this returning visitor exposed to stripping?
